video.title: Security principles and threat modelling: Saltzer and Schroeder, and STRIDE
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Joseph - computer science lecturer, Nairobi
Prof Farah - head of department, Amman
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: A university once left a storage bucket of student records open to the internet. No one hacked anything. A default setting was simply never changed.
Today: the classic design principles for secure systems, how STRIDE finds threats before attackers do, and how to teach both without a list to memorise.

Security aims at three properties. Confidentiality keeps data from the wrong people. Integrity keeps it from being changed without permission. Availability keeps it there when the right people need it.

In nineteen seventy five, Saltzer and Schroeder listed design principles that still hold. Fail-safe defaults mean deny unless allowed. Least privilege means give only what is needed. Complete mediation means check every access.
Industry breach reports repeatedly find that stolen credentials, phishing and misconfiguration start most incidents. Exotic exploits are a small share. That is a lesson for what we teach first.

Threat modelling asks what could go wrong before it does. Draw the data flows, mark trust boundaries, and walk each element through STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.

Principles taught as a list are forgotten by the exam. Instead, threat-model a system students use every day, like the university portal. Each team draws the data flow and finds one threat per STRIDE letter.
Quick check! The open bucket was readable by anyone because access was allowed until someone blocked it. Which principle did it break?
Fail-safe defaults. Access should be denied unless someone grants it on purpose. A secure system is safe before anyone configures it.
In the app, open the breach lab. Set up the five accounts, let the forum get hacked, and name the principle each defence applies.
Your turn. A student edits a hidden form field to change their grade before it is saved. Which STRIDE threat is that?
Tampering. Remember: deny by default, give least privilege, check every access, and use STRIDE on a real system before attackers do.

scenes.narration: Try it in your next lecture: give teams a one-page data flow of the course registration system. Each team must find one threat for every STRIDE letter and propose a fix.

checkpoints.prompt: The bucket was readable by anyone because access was allowed until someone blocked it. Which principle did it break?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: access should be denied unless granted on purpose.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the default allowed access; fail-safe defaults require deny unless allowed.

checkpoints.prompt: A student edits a hidden form field to change their grade before saving. Which STRIDE threat?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: modifying data without authorisation is tampering; validate on the server.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the student isn't pretending to be someone else; they are altering data, which is tampering.
